Dish Your Way · production brief

Production brief · for crew and suppliers · 13 October 2026

Dish Your Way: a cook-off series, eight episodes, three shoot days in Delhi.

This is the brief for the people we want to book: what the show is, how a shoot day runs, what the set and the food have to look like, and what we need from you by Wednesday. The client's name comes with the booking.

Harsh Arya · Ninety-Eight Entertainment · Delhi NCRArrow keys, scroll or swipe to move
The show

One dish, two home cooks, two kitchens under one window.

A branded series for a food brand, made by Ninety-Eight. Everything you need to quote is on these pages; the client, the host and the cooks are named when you are booked.

The format

One heritage dish an episode, cooked two ways by two home cooks from two states, side by side and in real time. A host opens the episode and asks each cook a question. Two tasters from the client taste blind and say which bowl they reached for, and why. No scores and no winner.

The count

Eight episodes, sixteen cooks, three shoot days: three episodes on 21 October, three on 12 November, two on 13 November. Six cooks a day, two at a time.

The output

For each episode: a 60-second vertical reel, a 6 to 8 minute episode for YouTube, two 15-second teasers, and stills for the grid. Eight of each.

The look

A traditional Indian kitchen, not modern and not a studio. Two matching cooking stations under one window, daylight as the key, plants, brass and clay. Page 5 is the set brief.

The product

The client makes ghee and cold-pressed oils. The product is in the cooking and never on the table as a prop: the same measure from the same jar goes into both pans, and the pour is the one shot that repeats in every episode.

Where

Delhi NCR. A farmhouse, a haveli or a kitchen studio; three places are being recced on 15 and 16 October and one is booked for all three days. Page 10 has them.

This brief is for the person it was sent to. Please do not forward it or post from the set; the client's name and the host's name are not public until the first episode is out.

A shoot day

A shoot day: three episodes in one window of daylight.

7:00
Crew call. The set checked; both stations laid identically, down to the spoon and the jar.
8:30
The day's six cooks arrive: the rule explained, mics on, a walk of the station. Nothing is cooked for the first time on camera; every recipe was tested the week before.
9:00 – 10:30
Episode A. Both cooks cook at once, in real time: about forty minutes on the pans, the rest for the stories to camera.
10:45
The tasting for A, blind, with both cooks in frame.
11:30 – 1:00
Episode B.
1:15
Tasting B, then lunch for everyone, from the two pots.
2:30 – 4:00
Episode C.
4:15
Tasting C, before the light goes: sunset is 5:45 on 21 October and 5:30 in November.
5:00
Stills of the dishes and the cooks for the grid. Wrap by 6.

The host's block

Two to three hours on 21 October, on the set: the opening and the dish announcement for all eight episodes, and questions to that day's cooks. For the November episodes the host's question to each cook is recorded to camera on this day and played to them at the station; they answer on camera.

Cameras

Three on the floor, two locked overheads, a macro for the pour and the tadka. Lavaliers on both cooks and the host; a boom on the pans.

Three days, eight episodes: 21 October for episodes 1 to 3, 12 November for 4 to 6, 13 November for 7 and 8. The November days can become one long day if the location allows a 7 am start and a lit tasting.
The set

A traditional kitchen, two stations, one window.

The look

Wood and stone surfaces, brass and kansa, clay and iron, a sil-batta, cane baskets, raw cotton, plants in terracotta. Gas burners dressed into a plinth, and a chulha for the roti episode. No steel island and no induction in frame.

The light

The window is the key light. The room's own fixtures go off; one soft neutral bounce opposite, so the ghee reads gold and the greens stay green. A daylight rig stands by for a cloudy day. The two overheads are locked.

The stations

Identical down to the pan, the spoon and the jar. The regional utensils are the only difference, and they are part of the story: a kansa thali and an uruli, a mitti ki handi and a lohe ki kadhai, a chakla and a tawa.

The food on camera

A macro lens for the pour and the tadka at 48 and 96 frames, a plating sequence before every tasting, sound up on the pan. The two kitchens are cut stage against stage: prep against prep, tadka against tadka, plate against plate.

The client's words for the look: traditional, not modern or lab-like; two stations; natural light, a window, plants.
Styling and set-up

Dressing the set, and running it in a farmhouse.

Food styling

The stylist, with an assistant, tests each recipe with its cook the week before, sources the ingredients, and plates for camera on the day. Sixteen recipes in all: six before 21 October, ten before 12 November.

Set dressing

The art director, with two dressers, builds the two stations on wooden tables with stone and brass tops, hires and buys the props across Delhi, and brings the plants. Dressed on Monday 19, struck the day after the last shoot day, and reset in three hours if the set moves.

Utensils

A house kit for both stations: pans, spoons, tongs, boards, the jar. Each cook brings one or two pieces of her own; the rest is hired by region.

The kitchen itself

Two gas burners a station on LPG with a safety person, running water to each station, a prep tent behind the set with a chest fridge and a hand-wash point, a food-safe check at the recce.

Outdoors or a farmhouse

A silent generator for the lights and the fridge. Shade cloth on the window side for a hard sun. A tent for the crew, and a room in the house as the cooks' green room. The house kitchen is the back kitchen. Pest, water and power checked at the recce.

Between the days

The set is dressed once. If one place holds all three days, three weeks apart, it is stored there; if not, one truck moves it in a morning.

What the production brings

Everything except the cook's recipe and the client's product: the stations, the props, the ingredients, the plates, the light, the sound, the meals.

What you tell us

What you need on site to do your part well, and anything in this plan you would do differently. We would rather hear it now than on Monday 19.

If you are quoting for styling or art, quote the tests and the build as their own lines, separate from the shoot days.

Shot by shot

Khichdi, Gujarat against Bengal, shot by shot.

The six beats of every episode, with what the camera does in each. The cooks cook in real time; the sixty seconds are cut from about forty minutes.

0–4s · The hook

Both cooks at their stations, the two-kitchens card over a two-shot, the host's line: the dish, the two states.

Camera

A locked wide on both stations, with a slow push in.

The food

Two pots, still empty. The jar between them.

4–12s · The two stories

A split screen of the two kitchens, one family line each to camera, hands already working.

Camera

An overhead above each station for the split; a camera on each face.

The food

Gujarat washes rice and moong together. Bengal dry-roasts the sona moong first. The difference starts here.

12–18s · The rule

Two measured spoons from one jar. "Bas do chamach ghee."

Camera

The macro lens on the spoon and the ghee going in. This is the product beat: three seconds, sound up, the same in every episode.

The food

The ghee blooms. Bengal fries potato and cauliflower in it; Gujarat holds its spoon back.

18–36s · The cook

Matched actions cut against each other, the clock in the corner, the host's one question to each cook.

Camera

The overheads on the pans; a third camera roams for hands and faces.

The food

Gujarat's pot goes soft and pale with turmeric. Bengal's takes bay leaf, ginger, cumin, a pinch of sugar and the fried vegetables, and turns golden.

36–52s · The blind taste

The two tasters in eye masks, two plain bowls marked A and B, the spoon, the pause. The cooks wait.

Camera

A camera on the tasters, the overheads on the bowls, the cooks' faces on the reverse.

The food

Served the same way in the same bowls. No garnish that gives a state away.

52–60s · The pick

The masks come off. She says which bowl she reached for, and why. Both cooks in frame; no score, no winner.

Camera

Back to the wide, then down to the dish.

The food

The two bowls side by side for the last frame, each with its state's name.

The six frames are direction frames, generated to set the look; nothing has been shot yet. Sound: lavaliers on both cooks and the host, a boom on the pans. Light: the window, or a daylight rig, so the ghee reads gold and not orange. Styling: brass and steel on the stations, and the jar by the stove, never in the centre.

Where

Where: three places under recce, and a studio if none of them works.

What it means for you

Open flame on set, a generator for power, water run to the stations, a prep tent with a fridge, and a 7 am call. The recce on 15 and 16 October settles which.

The National Crafts Museum

Its village complex at Pragati Maidan is the third place under recce: real village dwellings and courtyards, with the museum's own rules on fire and filming.

One place for three days

We want the same place on 21 October and 12 and 13 November, with the set stored between, so it is built once.

If you know a place

A home or a farm in Delhi NCR with a traditional kitchen and a window we have not seen: tell us, with a photo, by Wednesday.

Pictures from the venues' own listings and the channel named, shown as references only. The location is confirmed on Friday 16 October.
